metadata.title: Baseline programming diagnostic
metadata.summary: A low-stakes check of starting knowledge before Week 1 teaching. Not a formal OCR assessment and not a grade.

content.text: Before we start
This diagnostic helps you and your teacher see what you already know about software, data and input/output. It does not count toward Assignment 1 or P1.

content.prompt: Which of these is the best description of software used in a workplace?

options.label: A set of programs that store, process or present business information
Only the physical keyboard and screen

feedback.correct: Software is the programs a business uses to handle information.
feedback.incorrect: Think about programs that store or process information, not the hardware or paper records.

content.prompt: Which value is a Boolean?

feedback.correct: Boolean values are True or False.
feedback.incorrect: Boolean means True or False, not text or a number.

content.prompt: In Python, what does input() do?

options.label: Reads text typed by the user

feedback.correct: input() reads text from the user.
feedback.incorrect: print() displays output. input() reads what the user types.

content.prompt: Have you written a program before? If yes, which language? If no, write 'No previous programming'.
content.guidance: Thank you. This is a starting-point note for you and your teacher, not a mark.

metadata.title: Business data explorer

content.text: Businesses use software to take orders, store customer details, calculate prices and record whether a delivery is required. Those programs only work if each piece of data has an appropriate type.
A local supplier takes telephone orders. Classify each piece of order data.

content.prompt: Choose the most appropriate fundamental data type for each item.

feedback.correct: Name is text, quantity is a whole number, price may include pence, and delivery is yes/no.
feedback.incorrect: Ask: is it text, a whole number, a number that may include a fraction, or true/false?

content.prompt: Why is a floating point type more appropriate than an integer for a product price?
content.guidance: A price can include a fractional amount, such as 12.50. An integer can only store whole numbers.

metadata.title: Variables and fundamental data types
metadata.summary: Learn what a variable is and when to use integer, floating point, string and Boolean in a business program.

content.text: Unit 14 is internally assessed. Week 1 starts Assignment 1 (P1): explain universal programming constructs with worked examples. Completing this activity is practice, not P1 achieved.
A variable is a named store for a value. The type describes what kind of value it holds.

content.label: Read these Python examples, then add one more variable of your own.
content.starter:
customer_name = "Patel"
quantity = 3
unit_price = 12.5
delivery_required = True

content.prompt: Which fundamental type should store whether an invoice has been paid?

feedback.correct: Paid or not paid is a Boolean.
feedback.incorrect: A yes/no business fact is stored as Boolean.

content.prompt: In your own words, what is the difference between a variable and a value?
content.guidance: A value is the data itself (for example 3). A variable is the named store that holds that value.

content.prompt: What does input() return in Python?

feedback.correct: input() returns text. Week 2 looks at converting types in more depth.

metadata.title: First Python business-order program
metadata.summary: Create a simple program that asks for business-order information, stores it in variables and prints a formatted summary.

content.text: Ask for business-order information, store each piece in a variable with an appropriate type, and print a summary. Do not add Week 2 conversion work beyond the int() scaffold for quantity.

content.label: Python editor
content.instructions: Keep the four fundamental types in mind: name as string, quantity as integer, price as a number that may include pence, delivery as a yes/no fact. Enter sample values in Program input, then use Run to test.

# Business order — Week 1
# input() returns text. int() is used only so quantity is a whole number.

hints: Print a labelled summary of all four values.

metadata.title: Week 1 retrieval
metadata.summary: A short formative check of the four fundamental data types before conversion teaching.

content.text: Four fundamental types
Week 1 used integer, floating point, string and Boolean to store business data. This check is formative only. It is not a grade and is not P1.

content.prompt: Which value is a floating-point number?

feedback.correct: 12.50 is a floating-point number. Quotes would make it a string.
feedback.incorrect: A floating-point number includes a fractional part and is not wrapped in quotes.

content.prompt: Customer name "Ngọc Trần-García" should be stored as which type?

feedback.correct: Names are text, including accents, hyphens and more than one word.
feedback.incorrect: A name is text. Do not force it into a number or a true/false value.

content.prompt: Match each Week 1 business value to its fundamental type.

items.label: Unit price in pounds and pence

feedback.correct: Those four types are the Week 1 foundation for this week's conversion work.
feedback.incorrect: Quantity is a whole number, price may include pence, names are text, and delivery is yes/no.

content.title: Formative only
content.text: Correct options are stored in the hub for instant feedback. They are not secure assignment evidence.

metadata.title: Why conversion is necessary
metadata.summary: Show that input() returns a string and that "10" + "5" concatenates instead of adding.

content.text: input() returns text
Python input() always returns a string. If a cashier types 10, the program stores "10", not the integer 10. Arithmetic needs a numeric type first.

content.label: Read this example
content.instructions: This fragment shows the conversion problem. The browser does not run it. Predict the output, then answer below.
content.starter:
first = input("First quantity: ")   # learner types 10
second = input("Second quantity: ") # learner types 5
print(first + second)

content.prompt: If the user types 10 and then 5, what does print(first + second) display?

feedback.correct: The + operator concatenates strings, so "10" + "5" is "105".
feedback.incorrect: Both values are strings. + joins them as text rather than adding them as numbers.

content.prompt: Why must quantity be converted before it is used in arithmetic?

feedback.correct: Conversion is needed because input() returns text.
feedback.incorrect: print() can display numbers. The issue is that input() returns a string.

content.prompt: In one or two sentences, explain why a business program must convert quantity before calculating a total.
content.guidance: A typical answer mentions that typed input is text, and text cannot be multiplied or added as money or stock.

content.title: Unreliable input
content.text: Users type unexpected values. Treating all input as trusted numbers is a common source of defects. Convert deliberately, and expect invalid text.

metadata.title: Conversion functions
metadata.summary: Teach int(), float(), str() and bool(), including a deliberate conversion failure.

content.text: int, float, str and bool
Convert with int(), float(), str() and bool() before you calculate or store a typed value. Convert as close as possible to the input, then use the typed variable.

content.label: Worked conversion examples
content.instructions: Read these conversions. int("10") is 10. float("12.50") is 12.5. str(10) is "10". bool(0) is False; any non-zero number is True.
content.starter:
quantity = int(input("Quantity: "))
price = float(input("Unit price: "))
label = str(quantity)
flag = bool(quantity)

content.prompt: Which call is appropriate for a price typed as 12.50?

feedback.correct: Prices include pence, so float() is the matching conversion.
feedback.incorrect: int("12.50") raises ValueError. bool() would only test whether text was typed.

content.label: Deliberate failure
content.instructions: This program is meant to fail. Do not "fix" it here. Read the error you would see in Python, then interpret it below.
content.starter:
quantity = int(input("Quantity: "))
# If the user types ten, Python raises:
# ValueError: invalid literal for int() with base 10: 'ten'

content.prompt: A user types ten instead of 10. What happens, and what does the error tell you?
content.guidance: int() cannot convert the letters ten. Python raises ValueError. The program stops unless later weeks add handling.

content.title: bool() on text
content.text: bool("False") is True because the string is not empty. Do not use bool() to interpret the words True and False typed by a user.

content.label: Python editor
content.instructions: Convert quantity with int() and price with float() before any arithmetic. Use Run for formative checks where possible.
content.starter:
quantity_text = input("Quantity: ")
price_text = input("Unit price: ")
# Convert, then calculate a line total.

checks.passFeedback: int() and float() are present. Run the file in your Python environment to see conversion work or fail.
checks.failFeedback: Include int() for quantity and float() for price.

Customer records arrive messy: extra spaces, mixed case, commas in addresses. Predefined subroutines clean that text. Choose the operation that matches the job.

content.instructions: Read these examples. Keep legitimate names such as Mary-Anne, O'Neill and Ngọc. Do not strip hyphens or apostrophes just to make data simpler.
content.starter:
raw_name = "  jane smith  "
name = raw_name.strip().title()
email = "Jane.Smith@Example.com".lower()

postcode = "ls1 4ap".upper()

items.label: Remove leading and trailing spaces from a name
Store an email address in a consistent case
Display a UK postcode in capitals
Separate "12 High Street, Leeds" into street and city
Check that a product code is 8 characters long

feedback.correct: Each subroutine has a specific job. Matching the job to the call is the Week 2 skill.
feedback.incorrect: strip spaces, lower emails, upper postcodes, split on a separator, replace a substring, len for length.

metadata.title: Formatted business output
metadata.summary: Use f-strings to produce a professional receipt-style summary.

content.text: f-strings for business output
A receipt should be readable: labels, currency and two decimal places. f-strings place converted values into that layout.

content.label: Worked receipt
content.instructions: Read this receipt layout. Labels, currency and two decimal places sit in f-strings.
content.starter:
customer = "River Café"
subtotal = 18.5
vat = subtotal * 0.2
total = subtotal + vat
print(f"Customer: {customer}")
print(f"Subtotal: £{subtotal:.2f}")
print(f"VAT (20%): £{vat:.2f}")
print(f"Total: £{total:.2f}")

content.label: Python editor
content.instructions: Complete the receipt using an f-string. Include subtotal, VAT and total. Use Run to preview output where your code does not need typed input.
content.starter:
customer = "River Café"
subtotal = 18.5
vat_rate = 0.2
# Calculate VAT and total, then print a labelled receipt with f-strings.

checks.passFeedback: The receipt uses an f-string and business totals. Run it in Python to confirm the layout.
checks.failFeedback: Print with an f-string and include subtotal, VAT or total.

content.prompt: Why use an f-string on a receipt instead of joining several strings with + ?

options.label: It keeps labels and converted values in one readable line
It converts strings to integers automatically
It uploads the receipt to GitHub

feedback.correct: f-strings format values in place. They do not replace conversion.
feedback.incorrect: You still convert numbers first. f-strings only control how the output is written.

metadata.title: Reading and extending .gitignore
metadata.summary: Explain the supplied .gitignore, ignored generated files, and how to add an extra ignore rule.

content.text: Keep generated files out of Git
The Classroom repository includes a .gitignore. Git uses it to skip files that should not be committed: Python cache, virtual environments and editor settings.

Typical supplied entries include Python cache (__pycache__/, *.pyc), virtual environments (.venv/) and editor folders (.idea/, .vscode/). These are generated or local. They are not the business program. Committing them clutters history and can leak editor or machine-specific files.

content.prompt: Why should __pycache__/ stay out of the repository?

options.label: It is generated cache, not source the team should review
Python cannot run if the folder is ignored
GitHub deletes ignored folders from the classroom

feedback.correct: Cache is rebuilt locally. Source and .gitignore belong in Git; cache does not.
feedback.incorrect: Ignoring cache does not stop Python. It keeps the repository about the program.

content.label: .gitignore excerpt
content.instructions: This is not Python to run. Add one extra ignored entry such as .DS_Store or *.log under the comment.
content.starter:
__pycache__/
*.pyc
.venv/
.idea/
.vscode/
# Add one extra generated or local pattern below.

content.prompt: Which extra pattern did you add, and why should that file stay local?
content.guidance: A generated or machine-specific file (for example .DS_Store or a log) does not help another learner run the business program.

content.title: Clean repository
content.text: A professional repository contains source, tests and agreed config. After changing .gitignore, remove any already-tracked cache from the index in Git itself. This hub does not run Git.

metadata.title: Five conversion debugging programs
metadata.summary: Inspect five programs that fail because of missing or incorrect conversion, repair each one, and explain the cause.

content.text: Repair missing conversion
Each program is deliberately broken. Inspect the problem, repair it in the editor, use Run for formative checks, then explain the cause below.

content.label: Python editor
content.instructions: Program 1: two quantities are added as text. Convert both with int() before adding.
content.starter:
first = input("First quantity: ")
second = input("Second quantity: ")
print("Total items:", first + second)

checks.passFeedback: int() is present. In Python, 10 and 5 should now total 15, not 105.
checks.failFeedback: Convert both quantities with int() before adding.

content.prompt: Program 1: what went wrong before the repair?
content.guidance: + concatenated two strings. The values needed int() before numeric addition.

content.label: Python editor
content.instructions: Program 2: a price is multiplied by 1.2 without conversion. Use float().
content.starter:
price = input("Unit price: ")
print("Price including VAT:", price * 1.2)
hints: A string cannot be multiplied by 1.2.

checks.passFeedback: float() is present. Run it in Python to confirm VAT is calculated.
checks.failFeedback: Convert the price with float() before multiplying.

content.prompt: Program 2: why did price * 1.2 fail?
content.guidance: price was still a string. Python cannot multiply that string by 1.2. float() is required.

content.label: Python editor
content.instructions: Program 3: int() is the wrong conversion for a price with pence. Use float().
content.starter:
price = int(input("Unit price: "))  # user types 12.50
print("Price:", price)

checks.passFeedback: float() is present. int() is the wrong tool for 12.50.
checks.failFeedback: Replace int() with float() for a price that includes pence.

content.prompt: Program 3: what error does int("12.50") cause, and which conversion is correct?
content.guidance: ValueError: invalid literal for int(). float("12.50") is the matching conversion.

content.label: Python editor
content.instructions: Program 4: a typed age is compared with 18 without conversion. Use int().
content.starter:
age = input("Age: ")
print("Adult ticket:", age > 18)
hints: Python 3 cannot compare a string with an integer using >.

checks.passFeedback: int() is present. The comparison can now use a whole number.
checks.failFeedback: Convert age with int() before comparing with 18.

content.prompt: Program 4: why must age be converted before age > 18?
content.guidance: input() is a string. Comparing it with 18 is a type error. Convert with int() first.

content.label: Python editor
content.instructions: Program 5: bool() is the wrong conversion for the words True/False. Compare the text instead (for example member.lower() == "true").
content.starter:
member = input("Loyalty member (True/False): ")
print("Apply discount:", bool(member))
hints: bool("False") is True because the string is not empty.
Compare normalised text, such as member.lower() == "true".

checks.passFeedback: The program compares the typed words instead of using bool() on text.
checks.failFeedback: Do not rely on bool() for the words True and False. Compare the text.

content.prompt: Program 5: why is bool("False") the wrong fix?
content.guidance: Non-empty strings are True, so bool("False") is True. Compare the letters the user typed.

metadata.title: Assignment 1: conversion and subroutines

content.text: P1 notes this week

P1 asks you to show understanding of the programming constructs used to build software for business. This week add two constructs: data type conversion and predefined subroutines. Completing these boxes is not P1 achieved. Your teacher assesses the submitted technical guide.

For **each** construct record:

* an explanation
* its purpose
* a worked Python example
* why a business program needs it

content.prompt: Draft the conversion section: explanation, purpose, a short Python example, and a business reason.
Draft the predefined-subroutines section: explanation, purpose, a short Python example, and a business reason.

content.title: Not a grade
content.text: The hub never awards Pass, Merit or Distinction. Saving these notes does not mean P1 is achieved.

metadata.title: Homework: finish calculation and P1 notes
metadata.summary: Complete the directed independent study from the Scheme of Learning, with optional stretch for more confident learners.

content.text: Directed independent study

Finish the River Café calculation in your cloned repository if you did not complete it in Session 2. Convert input before arithmetic, print a receipt with f-strings, extend .gitignore if needed, and commit on your named feature branch. Then finish the Assignment 1 notes for conversion and predefined subroutines.

content.label: Python editor
content.instructions: Continue the calculation here if useful, but the assessed copy is the file in your GitHub repository. Use Program input with Run to test.
content.starter:
# Homework — finish the takeaway calculation
customer = input("Customer name: ")
quantity = int(input("Number of items: "))
unit_price = float(input("Unit price: "))
subtotal = quantity * unit_price
vat = subtotal * 0.2
total = subtotal + vat
print(f"{customer}: subtotal £{subtotal:.2f}, VAT £{vat:.2f}, total £{total:.2f}")
hints: Commit on feature/week-2-conversion or the name you chose.
Push to GitHub. The hub is not the repository.

checks.passFeedback: The homework program still converts and formats. Commit and push on GitHub, then complete the P1 drafts.
checks.failFeedback: Keep int(), float() and an f-string print.

content.prompt: Confirm what you committed (calculation, .gitignore change, P1 notes) and the branch name.

content.title: Stretch (optional)
content.text: More confident learners may try: try/except around a failed int() or float(); observe that int(19.99) truncates rather than rounding; and tidy commit history on the feature branch. These are not required Week 2 outcomes.

content.title: What next
content.text: Week 3 introduces selection. Do not start selection work yet. Keep Assignment 1 focused on conversion and predefined subroutines from this week.
